module_title: Scaling Up: From Small Press to Commercial Oil Mill

lessons.title: Assessing Your Readiness to Scale
lessons.body: Scaling from a small manual or motorised press to a commercial oil mill is a major business decision. It requires more than just buying bigger equipment. You must assess your current operations, market demand, financial capacity, and management skills. In Africa, many small-scale oil producers operate informally. To scale, you need to formalise your business, understand regulations, and secure reliable supply of raw materials. Start by evaluating your current production capacity. If you are producing 50 litres per day and selling everything you make, and you have consistent demand from wholesalers or processors, you may be ready to scale. But if your sales are irregular or you lack storage, scaling could lead to unsold stock and cash flow problems. Next, analyse your raw material supply. A commercial mill processing 1 tonne of groundnuts per day needs about 30 tonnes per month. Can your current suppliers meet that? Do you need contracts with farmers or aggregators? Consider seasonality. In many African countries, groundnuts, sunflower, and palm fruit are seasonal. You need to plan for storage or source from multiple regions. Financial readiness is critical. Scaling requires capital for equipment, installation, working capital, and possibly a new site. Explore financing options: bank loans, microfinance, grants, or investor partnerships. Prepare a business plan showing projected revenues, costs, and profits. Include a sensitivity analysis for price fluctuations. Management capacity is often overlooked. A commercial mill needs staff for procurement, production, quality control, sales, and administration. Do you have the skills to manage a larger team? If not, plan to hire or train. Also, consider legal and regulatory requirements. Register your business, obtain tax identification, and comply with food safety and environmental regulations. In many African countries, edible oil production is regulated by standards bureaus. Your product may need certification. Finally, think about infrastructure. Do you have reliable electricity or fuel for machinery? Is your site accessible for trucks? Do you have water for processing and cleaning? Answering these questions honestly will tell you if you are ready to scale. If not, take steps to fill the gaps before investing in expensive equipment.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Equipment for a Commercial Oil Mill
lessons.body: The equipment you choose determines your production capacity, oil yield, quality, and operating costs. For a commercial oil mill, you need a series of machines: cleaning, dehulling, grinding, pressing, filtering, and packaging. The type and size depend on your raw material and desired output. For oilseeds like groundnuts, sunflower, and sesame, you typically use a screw press or expeller. These come in various capacities, from 1 tonne per day to 20 tonnes per day. A screw press works by crushing the seed and applying pressure to squeeze out oil. It is robust and suitable for continuous operation. However, it generates heat, which can affect oil quality. For high-value oils, you might use a cold press, which operates at lower temperatures but yields less oil. For palm fruit, you need a different setup: steriliser, thresher, digester, press, and clarification. Palm oil mills are more complex and expensive. If you are processing copra or palm kernel, you need a kernel press. When selecting equipment, consider the following: capacity, efficiency, durability, ease of maintenance, and availability of spare parts. In Africa, importing equipment from China, India, or Europe is common. But import duties, shipping, and delays can add 30-50% to the cost. Local fabricators in countries like Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa can make screw presses, but quality varies. Always inspect a working machine before buying. Ask for a demonstration with your raw material. Check the oil yield: a good screw press should extract 90-95% of the oil from groundnuts. Also, consider the power source. Electric motors are common, but in rural areas with unreliable electricity, you may need a diesel engine. Some mills use a combination. Automation level is another choice. Manual feeding and discharge are labour-intensive but cheaper. Semi-automatic machines with conveyors and pumps increase throughput but require more capital. For a commercial mill, semi-automation is usually the minimum. Don't forget auxiliary equipment: boilers for heating, filters (plate and frame or vacuum), storage tanks, and filling machines. A filter press removes impurities and extends shelf life. Storage tanks should be food-grade stainless steel or coated to prevent rust. Packaging can be manual or automatic. For small commercial mills, manual filling into jerrycans or bottles is fine, but for branded retail, you need a filling and capping machine. Finally, plan for maintenance. Keep a stock of critical spares: seals, bearings, screens, and belts. Train your operators on daily cleaning and lubrication. A well-maintained machine lasts 10-15 years. Buying the right equipment is a balance between cost and capability. Don't overbuy; match capacity to your market and supply. But also don't underbuy; a machine that breaks down constantly will cost you more in downtime and lost sales.

lessons.title: Financing Your Expansion: Options and Strategies
lessons.body: Scaling up requires significant capital. In Africa, accessing finance is often the biggest hurdle for small and medium enterprises. But there are options. First, calculate how much you need. Include equipment purchase, installation, site preparation, working capital for raw materials and salaries, and contingency. A commercial oil mill with 2 tonnes per day capacity might cost $50,000 to $150,000, depending on location and automation. Where can you get this money? Personal savings and reinvested profits are the cheapest. If you have been operating a small press, you may have savings. Family and friends can provide soft loans, but be clear on terms to avoid conflict. Microfinance institutions (MFIs) offer loans up to $10,000 or more, but interest rates can be high (20-40% per year). They often require collateral or group guarantees. Commercial banks lend to registered businesses with collateral, usually land or buildings. Interest rates vary: 10-25% in many African countries. Prepare a solid business plan and financial statements. Banks want to see cash flow projections showing you can repay. Development finance institutions (DFIs) and impact investors are interested in agribusiness. Organisations like the African Development Bank, IFC, and various funds provide loans or equity to SMEs. They may offer lower interest and longer tenures but require rigorous reporting. Grants are available from NGOs, government agencies, and international donors. For example, the African Development Bank's Feed Africa initiative, or USAID's Feed the Future. Grants don't need repayment but are competitive. Look for matching grants where you contribute a portion. Equipment leasing is another option. You pay a monthly fee to use the machine, and at the end of the lease, you may own it. This preserves cash for working capital. Supplier credit: some equipment suppliers allow you to pay a deposit and the balance over 12-24 months. Negotiate this. Value chain financing: off-takers (buyers) may advance funds or guarantee a loan if you have a supply contract. For example, a supermarket chain might finance your packaging machine if you agree to supply them. Crowdfunding and peer-to-peer lending are emerging in Africa. Platforms like Kiva, M-Changa, and Lendahand connect you with individual lenders. But you need a compelling story and transparent use of funds. Government schemes: many African governments have agricultural development banks or funds. In Nigeria, the Bank of Agriculture; in Kenya, the Agricultural Finance Corporation. They offer concessional loans. Before approaching any lender, prepare: a business plan, cash flow projections, collateral documents, and personal identification. Be honest about your track record. If you have defaulted before, it will show. Build a relationship with your bank. Start with a small loan and repay on time to build credit history. Also, consider equity investors. They provide capital in exchange for shares. You lose some ownership but gain expertise and networks. Angel investors and venture capital firms are increasingly active in African agribusiness. Finally, don't forget internal financing. Improve efficiency to generate more cash. Reduce waste, negotiate better prices for raw materials, and increase sales. Sometimes you can scale in phases: buy one machine, increase production, save, then buy the next. This is slower but safer. Whichever route you choose, avoid over-borrowing. Debt repayments should not exceed 30-40% of your monthly net cash flow. Stress-test your plan: what if raw material prices rise 20%? What if sales drop 30%? If you can survive, proceed.

lessons.title: Setting Up Your Commercial Oil Mill: Location, Layout, and Utilities
lessons.body: Location and layout are critical for efficiency, safety, and compliance. A commercial oil mill needs space for raw material storage, processing, finished product storage, and waste management. Choose a site with good access roads for trucks, reliable water and electricity, and room for expansion. In Africa, many mills are located near raw material sources to reduce transport costs. But if your market is in the city, you might locate near the market to reduce distribution costs. Balance both. The site should be at least 500 square metres for a small commercial mill. It should be fenced and secure. Avoid flood-prone areas. Check local zoning laws: some areas are residential only. You need permission from local authorities. Layout should follow a logical flow: raw materials enter, are cleaned, processed, and move to packaging without backtracking. This reduces handling and contamination. Designate areas: receiving bay, cleaning section, dehulling, grinding, pressing, filtering, storage tanks, packaging, finished goods store, and waste area. Keep food contact surfaces separate from waste. Ensure there is a changing area for staff and toilets. Utilities: electricity is essential. A 10-tonne per day mill may need 50-100 kW. If the grid is unreliable, install a diesel generator or solar system. Solar is expensive upfront but cheap to run. Water: you need clean water for cleaning and possibly for processing (e.g., palm oil clarification). A borehole or municipal supply is fine. Test water quality. Steam or heating: some processes need heat, like conditioning seeds before pressing. You can use a boiler fired by biomass (wood, husks) or diesel. Ensure proper ventilation. Compressed air may be needed for pneumatic controls. Waste management: oil production generates solid waste (cake, husks, shells) and liquid waste (wash water). Cake is valuable as animal feed. Husks can be burned for energy. Liquid waste must be treated before discharge. Construct a soakaway or septic system. Comply with environmental regulations. Safety: install fire extinguishers, first aid kit, and eye wash. Machinery should have guards. Train staff on safety. Also, consider noise and dust. Use dust extraction systems in cleaning and grinding. Noise from presses can be high; provide ear protection. Office and laboratory: you need a small office for administration and a lab for quality testing (moisture, free fatty acids, peroxide value). Basic lab equipment: moisture meter, titration set, oven, balance. Finally, think about future expansion. Leave space for additional presses or storage. A well-planned site saves money and headaches later.

lessons.title: Managing Raw Material Supply at Scale
lessons.body: A commercial oil mill lives or dies by its raw material supply. You need a consistent, affordable, and quality supply of oilseeds or palm fruit. At small scale, you might buy from local markets. At commercial scale, you need contracts with farmers, aggregators, or cooperatives. Start by identifying your raw material catchment area. How far can you source without transport costs eating your margin? For groundnuts, a radius of 100-200 km is typical. For palm fruit, 50-100 km because it perishes quickly. Map out suppliers: smallholder farmers, large farms, traders, and cooperatives. Build relationships. Visit them, understand their challenges, and offer fair prices. Consider providing inputs (seeds, fertiliser) on credit to farmers in exchange for exclusive supply. This is contract farming. It benefits both: you get reliable supply, they get a market. But it requires trust and enforcement. In many African countries, contract farming is informal. Write simple agreements specifying quantity, quality, price, and delivery schedule. Quality matters. High-quality raw materials yield more oil and better quality. Test for moisture content (should be below 10% for groundnuts), foreign matter, and damaged kernels. Reject mouldy or insect-damaged seeds. Aflatoxin is a major concern in groundnuts and maize. Test for it. If you buy aflatoxin-contaminated seeds, your oil may be unsafe. Set up a buying station with weighing scales, moisture meters, and aflatoxin test kits. Train your buyers to inspect. Pricing: offer a price that reflects quality. Premium for low moisture and low aflatoxin. This incentivises farmers to improve. Also, consider seasonality. Groundnuts are harvested once or twice a year. You need to buy enough to last until next harvest. That means storage. Build a warehouse with proper ventilation, pallets, and pest control. Fumigate if necessary. For palm fruit, you need to process within 24-48 hours of harvest. So you need daily collection routes. Logistics: own or hire trucks. For groundnuts, a 10-tonne truck can collect from multiple villages. Plan routes to minimise empty runs. Use tracking to monitor. Also, consider processing raw materials into intermediate products. For example, you can buy groundnut cake from small presses and extract residual oil. This is a secondary source. Finally, diversify. Don't rely on one crop or one region. If groundnut prices spike, you can switch to sunflower or sesame. But that requires flexible equipment. In summary, secure supply through contracts, quality control, storage, and logistics. It is the backbone of your commercial mill.

lessons.title: Operations, Quality Control, and Staffing for a Commercial Mill
lessons.body: Running a commercial oil mill requires systems for operations, quality control, and human resources. Without these, you will have inconsistent product, unhappy customers, and high staff turnover. Operations: create a production schedule. Based on sales orders and raw material availability, plan daily, weekly, and monthly production. Track key metrics: oil yield (litres per tonne), downtime, energy consumption, and labour productivity. Use simple record sheets or software. Conduct daily machine checks: lubrication, belt tension, temperature. Clean after each shift. Implement preventive maintenance: change oil, filters, and worn parts on schedule. Keep a spare parts inventory. Quality control: from raw material to finished oil, test at each stage. Raw material: moisture, foreign matter, aflatoxin. During processing: temperature, pressure, and residence time. Finished oil: free fatty acid (FFA), peroxide value, colour, and moisture. FFA indicates hydrolysis; high FFA means poor quality or old oil. Peroxide value indicates oxidation; high peroxide means rancidity. Set specifications: for example, FFA below 0.5% for refined oil, below 2% for crude. If your oil exceeds limits, investigate and correct. Keep samples from each batch for traceability. If a customer complains, you can test the retained sample. Also, ensure hygiene: staff wear clean uniforms, hairnets, and gloves. Equipment is sanitised. Water used in processing is potable. Packaging: use food-grade containers. Label correctly with production date, batch number, and expiry. Staffing: a commercial mill needs a team. Key roles: production manager, machine operators, quality control officer, procurement officer, sales and marketing officer, accountant, and general workers. In small mills, one person may do multiple roles. But as you scale, separate duties to avoid fraud and errors. Hire based on skills and attitude. Train continuously. Operators need technical training on the specific machines. Quality control staff need training on testing methods. Sales staff need training on customer service and negotiation. Pay fair wages and on time. Provide incentives for good performance, like bonuses for high yield or zero defects. Create a safe and respectful work environment. Address grievances. Keep records of employment, contracts, and payroll. Comply with labour laws: minimum wage, working hours, leave, and social security. Consider hiring women and youth; they are often overlooked but can be reliable. Finally, lead by example. If you are disciplined and quality-focused, your team will follow. A well-run mill is a profitable mill.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Operating a Commercial Oil Mill in Africa â Yields, Costs, Quality, and Safety

This lesson is the desk-side reference you keep on the wall of the mill office. It converts the earlier modules â readiness, equipment, financing, site setup, raw material supply, and operations â into the numbers, standards, and checks you will actually use every day. The focus is commercial: what yields you should expect, what it costs to run, how quality is judged in the market, and how to keep your staff and customers safe. Figures are drawn from FAO, ILRI, WHO and university extension sources, with African market context throughout.

Read it once end-to-end, then use it as a look-up sheet. Every table and diagram is designed to be printed, laminated, and pinned near the press or the weighing scale.

1. Realistic Extraction Yields by Crop

The single most important number in your business plan is the extraction rate. It determines how much raw material you buy, how much oil you sell, and how much cake you can sell as a second revenue stream. The table below gives typical mechanical expeller yields for common African oil crops. Note that yields vary with variety, moisture, and the condition of your press.

Table 1: Typical mechanical (expeller) oil extraction rates for common African oil crops
Oil crop Oil content of seed (%) Typical expeller yield (litres/100 kg seed) Residual oil in cake (%) Main African producing regions
Groundnut (shelled) 45â52 38â45 6â10 Senegal, Nigeria, Sudan, Malawi
Sesame 48â55 40â46 7â11 Ethiopia, Sudan, Nigeria, Tanzania
Sunflower 38â45 32â38 8â12 Tanzania, Uganda, Kenya, Zambia
Palm kernel 45â50 36â42 6â9 Nigeria, Ghana, CÃ´te d'Ivoire, DRC
Coconut (copra) 60â68 50â58 6â10 Ghana, Tanzania, Mozambique, Kenya
Soya bean 18â22 12â16 4â7 Nigeria, Zambia, South Africa, Uganda

Sources: FAO, Small-scale oil extraction from groundnuts and copra; FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius, Standard for Named Vegetable Oils (CXS 210-1999); ILRI small-scale agro-processing notes; University extension publications on oilseed processing.

Business implication: If you buy 1,000 kg of groundnut at USD 0.60/kg (USD 600) and achieve a 42% yield, you produce about 420 litres of oil. At a wholesale price of USD 2.20/litre, that is USD 924 in oil revenue â plus roughly 550 kg of cake at USD 0.20/kg (USD 110). Gross revenue is about USD 1,034 against USD 600 of raw material, before labour, energy, and overheads. The margin is real, but it is thin enough that a 5% yield loss wipes out most of your profit. This is why moisture control and press maintenance are not optional.

2. Operating Cost and Margin Benchmarks

Costs vary widely across Africa, but the structure of a commercial oil mill is consistent. The table below gives indicative cost shares for a mill processing 1â2 tonnes of seed per day, based on FAO and ILRI small-scale processing data and typical African SME experience.

Table 2: Indicative cost structure and margin for a 1â2 t/day oil mill (share of total operating cost)
Cost category Typical share of operating cost Key drivers Management lever
Raw material purchase 65â78% Farm-gate price, seasonality, moisture content Contract farming, off-season storage
Labour (production + admin) 8â12% Number of shifts, skill level Cross-training, piece-rate for pressing
Energy (diesel/electricity) 5â10% Press motor size, hours of operation Solar hybrid, scheduled pressing batches
Packaging and labelling 4â7% Bottle/jerrycan type, label quality Bulk sales to wholesalers, refillable containers
Maintenance and spares 2â4% Press wear parts, filter cloth Preventive maintenance schedule
Transport and distribution 2â5% Distance to market, vehicle ownership Cluster deliveries, third-party logistics
Licensing, testing, compliance 1â3% National standards, aflatoxin testing Batch testing, shared lab services

Sources: FAO, Small-scale oil extraction from groundnuts and copra; ILRI, Small-scale agro-processing and market access; University extension budgets for oilseed processing enterprises.

Business implication: Raw material dominates your cost base. That means your negotiating power with farmers and aggregators is your most important commercial skill. A 10% reduction in raw material cost â through contract farming, bulk buying at harvest, or better moisture negotiation â can raise your net margin by more than 30%. Do not spend your energy chasing a 2% saving on packaging while ignoring a 10% opportunity in procurement.

â  SAFETY WARNING â AFLATOXIN AND FOOD SAFETY

Groundnut, maize, and cottonseed can carry aflatoxins, which are carcinogenic and regulated in all export and most domestic markets. Never press mouldy, discoloured, or damp seed. Aflatoxin is not destroyed by normal cooking or pressing temperatures.

  • Test every incoming batch of groundnut and maize-based raw material for aflatoxin before acceptance.
  • Reject any lot with visible mould, musty smell, or moisture above 10%.
  • Store raw material on pallets in a dry, ventilated store; never on bare concrete or against walls.
  • Keep a batch record linking every finished oil container to its raw material lot, so you can trace and recall if needed.
  • Follow national food safety authority requirements and WHO/FAO Codex maximum levels for aflatoxins in oilseeds and edible oils.

3. Quality Standards Your Buyers Will Check

Commercial buyers â supermarkets, hotels, food processors, and exporters â judge oil on a small number of measurable parameters. Know them before you sign a supply contract.

  • Free Fatty Acid (FFA): A measure of oil breakdown. Good quality crude groundnut or sunflower oil should be below 1â2% FFA. High FFA means poor raw material or delayed processing.
  • Peroxide value: Indicates oxidation and rancidity. Lower is better; fresh oil should be well within Codex limits.
  • Moisture and volatile matter: Should be below 0.2% in finished oil. Residual water shortens shelf life.
  • Colour and clarity: Buyers expect a consistent, clean appearance. Filtration and settling matter commercially, not just aesthetically.
  • Aflatoxin level: Must be within national and Codex limits. This is a legal requirement, not a preference.
  • Packaging integrity: Food-grade containers, clean filling, tamper-evident seals, and legible labels with batch code and production date.

4. Quick Reference Checklist

Print this and pin it at the intake bay and the press. It is the minimum daily discipline for a commercial mill.

  1. Weigh and sample every delivery. Record supplier, weight, moisture, and visual condition before offloading.
  2. Reject mouldy or high-moisture raw material. No exceptions â aflatoxin risk is a business-ending risk.
  3. Clean the press and change filter cloth on schedule. Dirty equipment lowers yield and contaminates flavour.
  4. Check press temperature and cake residual oil daily. Rising residual oil means worn parts or wrong settings.
  5. Test FFA and moisture on every production batch. Record results; trend them weekly.
  6. Label every container with batch code and date. This is your traceability and your defence in a recall.
  7. Store oil in a cool, dark, dry place. Heat and light accelerate rancidity and shorten shelf life.
  8. Keep a maintenance and safety log. Guards in place, gloves worn, food-grade lubricants only, waste oil segregated.

5. Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-scale oil extraction from groundnuts and copra (FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin; free full text).
  • FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius â Standard for Named Vegetable Oils (CXS 210-1999) and related food safety standards.
  • WHO â Mycotoxins fact sheet (aflatoxin health risks and control).
  • ILRI â International Livestock Research Institute (small-scale agro-processing, feed and oil cake utilisation in Africa).
  • South Africa Department of Agriculture â extension publications on oilseed processing (practical enterprise budgets and crop guides).

This practical reference is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course Cooking Oil Production, Module 11. Use it with the earlier modules on readiness, equipment, financing, site setup, raw material supply, and operations. Figures are indicative and should be adjusted to your local market, currency, and national standards.

quiz.q: What is the first step before scaling up a small oil press to a commercial mill?
options: A) Buy the largest machine available
B) Assess your readiness in terms of supply, market, finance, and management
C) Hire more staff immediately
D) Borrow money from a bank
quiz.explanation: Assessing readiness ensures you have the necessary supply, demand, capital, and skills before investing in expensive equipment.

quiz.q: Which type of press is most common for oilseeds like groundnuts and sunflower at commercial scale?
options: A) Hydraulic press
B) Screw press or expeller
C) Bridge press
D) Manual ram press
quiz.explanation: Screw presses are robust, continuous, and suitable for a range of oilseeds, making them the standard for commercial mills.

quiz.q: Why is contract farming useful for a commercial oil mill?
options: A) It guarantees a reliable supply of raw materials
B) It eliminates the need for quality control
C) It reduces the need for storage
D) It allows you to pay farmers after selling oil
quiz.explanation: Contract farming provides a consistent supply of raw materials and a market for farmers, reducing uncertainty for both parties.

quiz.q: What does a high free fatty acid (FFA) level in crude oil indicate?
options: A) Good quality oil
B) Poor quality or old oil
C) High vitamin content
D) Proper refining
quiz.explanation: FFA indicates hydrolysis of triglycerides, which occurs due to poor handling, storage, or ageing, leading to lower quality.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key consideration when choosing a site for a commercial oil mill?
options: A) Proximity to a residential area
B) Access to reliable utilities and raw materials
C) Low land cost only
D) Availability of cheap labour only
quiz.explanation: Reliable utilities (water, electricity) and access to raw materials are critical for efficient operations and cost control.

quiz.q: What is aflatoxin and why is it a concern in oil production?
options: A) A type of oilseed
B) A toxic substance produced by moulds that can contaminate groundnuts and other crops
C) A machine used in filtering
D) A method of oil extraction
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin is a carcinogenic toxin produced by Aspergillus moulds, often found in poorly stored groundnuts, and can carry over into oil.

quiz.q: Which financing option does NOT require repayment?
options: A) Bank loan
B) Microfinance loan
C) Grant
D) Equipment leasing
quiz.explanation: Grants are funds provided by donors or governments that do not need to be repaid, unlike loans or leases.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum percentage of monthly net cash flow that should go to debt repayment?
quiz.explanation: Keeping debt repayments at 30-40% of net cash flow ensures you have enough working capital and a buffer for unexpected costs.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep retained samples from each production batch?
options: A) To sell later at a higher price
B) For traceability and quality investigation if a customer complains
C) To use as animal feed
D) To reduce waste
quiz.explanation: Retained samples allow you to test and verify quality if there is a complaint or recall, helping you identify and fix issues.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of using a screw press over a manual press?
options: A) Lower capital cost
B) Higher oil yield and continuous operation
C) No need for maintenance
D) Requires less skill to operate
quiz.explanation: Screw presses extract more oil and can run continuously, increasing throughput and profitability compared to manual presses.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a readiness assessment before scaling a small oil press to a commercial mill?
options: A) To determine if you can secure a bank loan
B) To evaluate whether your resources, market, and skills can support a larger operation
C) To calculate the exact price of a new oil expeller
D) To decide which country to import equipment from
quiz.explanation: A readiness assessment checks whether your finances, supply chain, technical skills, and market demand can sustain commercial-scale production.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key financial indicator that a small oil press is ready to scale?
options: A) You have more than one customer
B) You have consistent positive cash flow and retained earnings for reinvestment
C) You own a vehicle
D) You have been operating for at least one month
quiz.explanation: Consistent positive cash flow and retained earnings show the business can support the debt or investment needed for expansion.

quiz.q: When choosing a commercial oil expeller, why is seed preparation equipment such as cleaners and dehullers important?
options: A) It makes the oil taste better
B) It reduces wear on the expeller and improves oil yield and quality
C) It is required by law in all African countries
D) It replaces the need for a filter press
quiz.explanation: Cleaning and dehulling remove impurities and hard shells that cause wear and lower oil recovery, improving both yield and quality.

quiz.q: A commercial mill processes 2 tonnes of groundnuts per day at 42 percent oil content. If the expeller recovers 90 percent of the oil, how many kg of oil are produced daily?
options: A) 756 kg
B) 840 kg
C) 420 kg
D) 900 kg
quiz.explanation: 2,000 kg x 0.42 = 840 kg oil; 840 x 0.90 = 756 kg recovered oil per day.

quiz.q: Which financing option typically requires giving up some ownership or control of the business?
options: A) Bank term loan
B) Equity investor
C) Equipment lease
D) Supplier credit
quiz.explanation: An equity investor provides capital in exchange for a share of ownership and often some decision-making influence.

quiz.q: Why might a lease-to-own arrangement be attractive for an African oil mill expanding on a limited budget?
options: A) It avoids all interest and fees
B) It allows use of equipment with lower upfront capital while building ownership
C) It removes the need for raw materials
D) It guarantees higher oil prices
quiz.explanation: Lease-to-own reduces the initial cash outlay and spreads payments, making expansion possible without large upfront capital.

quiz.q: What is a major advantage of locating a commercial oil mill near raw material production areas?
options: A) Lower electricity tariffs
B) Reduced transport costs and fresher seed supply
C) Easier access to imported spare parts
D) Higher government subsidies
quiz.explanation: Proximity to farms lowers transport costs, reduces spoilage, and helps secure a steady supply of fresh seed.

quiz.q: In mill layout, why should the oil extraction area be separated from the packaging and storage area?
options: A) To reduce noise for workers
B) To prevent contamination and improve food safety
C) To make the building look bigger
D) To comply with export rules only
quiz.explanation: Separating extraction from packaging and storage reduces the risk of contaminating finished oil with dust, fumes, or pests.

quiz.q: What utility is often the most critical constraint for a commercial oil mill in rural Africa?
options: A) Reliable electricity or alternative power
B) Cable television
C) Air conditioning
D) Swimming pool water
quiz.explanation: Expellers, motors, and pumps need dependable power; unreliable grid electricity often forces mills to invest in generators or solar systems.

quiz.q: What is a practical strategy to manage raw material supply at scale?
options: A) Buy only from one large trader
B) Contract with multiple farmer groups and use warehouse receipts
C) Wait until prices are highest to buy
D) Stop buying during harvest season
quiz.explanation: Diversifying suppliers through contracts and warehouse receipts spreads risk and stabilises supply and prices.

quiz.q: If a mill needs 30 tonnes of copra per week and each farmer can supply 500 kg per week, how many farmers are needed?
options: A) 30 farmers
B) 60 farmers
C) 15 farmers
D) 45 farmers
quiz.explanation: 30,000 kg divided by 500 kg per farmer equals 60 farmers.

quiz.q: Why is moisture content testing important when buying oilseeds at scale?
options: A) High moisture increases oil yield
B) High moisture can cause mould, reduce oil quality, and lower extraction efficiency
C) It changes the colour of the seed only
D) It has no effect on storage
quiz.explanation: Excess moisture promotes mould and aflatoxins, and it reduces the efficiency of oil extraction and the shelf life of the oil.

quiz.q: Which quality control practice is most important for a commercial mill aiming to sell to formal markets?
options: A) Testing only the first batch of the day
B) Regular testing of free fatty acid, moisture, and impurities in oil
C) Relying on smell and colour alone
D) Skipping filtration to save time
quiz.explanation: Formal buyers and regulators require documented tests such as FFA, moisture, and impurity levels to ensure consistent quality.

quiz.q: What staffing approach is most suitable for a growing commercial oil mill?
options: A) Hire only family members regardless of skill
B) Define roles for production, quality, maintenance, and sales, and train staff
C) Use one person for all tasks indefinitely
D) Hire temporary workers with no training
quiz.explanation: Clear roles and trained staff improve efficiency, safety, and quality control as the operation grows.

quiz.q: A mill produces 500 litres of crude oil per day. If refining and packaging losses are 8 percent, how many litres of refined oil are available for sale daily?
options: A) 460 litres
B) 480 litres
C) 450 litres
D) 500 litres
quiz.explanation: 500 litres x 0.92 = 460 litres after 8 percent loss.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes the role of a feasibility study in scaling up?
options: A) It guarantees profits
B) It assesses technical, financial, and market viability before committing funds
C) It replaces the need for a business plan
D) It is only needed for export businesses
quiz.explanation: A feasibility study examines whether the proposed commercial mill is technically possible, financially viable, and market-supported.

quiz.q: Why is spare parts availability a critical factor when selecting commercial oil milling equipment in Africa?
options: A) It affects the colour of the machine
B) Long downtime without parts can cause major financial losses
C) It determines the taste of the oil
D) It is only important for export markets
quiz.explanation: If spare parts are hard to import, a breakdown can halt production for weeks, causing lost revenue and spoiled raw materials.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using a warehouse receipt system for raw material procurement?
options: A) It eliminates all storage costs
B) It allows farmers to store and use receipts as collateral while mills secure supply
C) It guarantees free transport
D) It removes the need for quality testing
quiz.explanation: Warehouse receipts give farmers access to credit and give mills a documented, secure way to buy and store seed.

quiz.q: A commercial mill plans to process 10 tonnes of sesame per day at 50 percent oil content with 85 percent recovery. What is the daily oil output?
quiz.explanation: 10,000 kg x 0.50 = 5,000 kg oil; 5,000 x 0.85 = 4,250 kg recovered oil per day.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common mistake when scaling from a small press to a commercial mill?
options: A) Training staff before starting production
B) Expanding capacity without securing enough raw material supply
C) Testing oil quality regularly
D) Keeping maintenance records
quiz.explanation: Many mills fail because they invest in larger equipment but cannot source enough seed to run it at profitable capacity.
